captions.instagram:
How is a dosa made?

A dosa is one ladle of sour batter turned into a crisp golden sheet in ninety seconds. Flick water on the tawa and watch the drops dance, walk the ladle out in a spiral to a film one millimetre thick, then cook it yourself: steam out through the lace, a crust climbing from the iron, and browning that cannot start until the base is dry.

→ A dosa is rice, urad dal and water, fermented overnight. Cut one open: a crisp brown base, a lace of holes, a soft pale top.
→ A dosa tawa is a heavy slab of iron. Flick water on it: under about 200 °C the drops hiss and vanish in a second.
→ Hotter still, the drops float on their own steam and dance for a minute. That is the Leidenfrost effect, and it means: too hot.
→ One ladle, one spiral, three seconds. 70 mL spread to a 13 cm radius makes a film just 1.3 mm thick.
→ On the tawa the film hits 100 °C in seconds. Water boils out as steam through the holes the ferment left.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/dosaclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How is a dosa made? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A dosa is one ladle of sour batter turned into a crisp golden sheet in ninety seconds. Flick water on the tawa and watch the drops dance, walk the ladle out in a spiral to a film one millimetre thick, then cook it yourself: steam out through the lace, a crust climbing from the iron, and browning that cannot start until the base is dry.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/dosaclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/dosaclear

In this video:
• Batter, a crisp side and a soft side. Dosa batter is rice and urad dal ground wet, thinned to about 70% water and fermented overnight by wild lactic acid bacteria, which sour it and fill it with gas.
• The tawa and the dancing drops. A 3 kg cast-iron tawa stores about 1.4 kJ for every degree, so cold batter does not chill it.
• One ladle, one spiral. Thickness is volume divided by area: 70 mL spread to a 13 cm radius is a film 1.3 mm thick.
• Steam out, crust up, colour in. While any batter is wet it is pinned at 100 °C, because the heat goes into steam (2,257 J per gram) that escapes through the holes.
• Why the first fails and the last goes soft. Wet batter glues itself into the pores of bare iron.
• A family, not one dish. Spread the same batter to half a millimetre and it is a paper roast; pour it thick and it is a set dosa or an uttapam.
